q: What is virtue?
a: Virtue is a constant disposition of the soul to do good.

q: How many kinds of virtue are there?
a: There are two kinds of virtue: the natural virtues, which we acquire by repeating good acts, such as those called moral; and the supernatural virtues, which we cannot acquire and cannot even exercise by our own forces alone, but which are given to us by God, and which are the virtues proper to the Christian.

q: What are the virtues proper to the Christian?
a: The virtues proper to the Christian are the supernatural virtues, and especially faith, hope, and charity, which are called theological or divine, because they have God Himself as their object and motive.

q: How do we receive and exercise the supernatural virtues?
a: We receive the supernatural virtues together with sanctifying grace, by means of the sacraments or by the love of charity, and we exercise them with the actual graces of good thoughts and inspirations by which God moves and helps us in every good act.

q: Among the supernatural virtues, which is the most excellent?
a: Among the supernatural virtues, the most excellent is charity, because it is inseparable from sanctifying grace, unites us intimately to God and to our neighbor, moves us to the perfect observance of the Law and to every good work, and will never cease: in it lies Christian perfection. Faith

q: What is faith?
a: Faith is that supernatural virtue by which we believe, on the authority of God, what He has revealed and proposes to us to be believed through the Church.

q: Where is preserved that which God has revealed and proposes to us to be believed through the Church?
a: That which God has revealed and proposes to us to be believed through the Church is preserved in Sacred Scripture and in Tradition.

q: What is Sacred Scripture?
a: Sacred Scripture is the collection of the books written by inspiration of God in the Old and the New Testament, and received by the Church as the work of God Himself.

q: What is Tradition?
a: Tradition is the teaching of Jesus Christ and of the Apostles, given by living voice, and transmitted by the Church to us without alteration.

q: Who can with authority make known to us, fully and in their true sense, the truths contained in Scripture and in Tradition?
a: The Church alone can with authority make known to us, fully and in their true sense, the truths contained in Scripture and in Tradition; for to her alone God entrusted the deposit of Faith, and sent the Holy Spirit, who continually assists her, so that she may not err.

q: Is it enough to believe in general the truths revealed by God?
a: It is not enough to believe in general the truths revealed by God; some — namely, the existence of God the Rewarder and the two principal mysteries — must also be believed by an explicit act of faith. 237 a. The two principal mysteries of the Faith are: 1. The Unity and Trinity of God; 2. The Incarnation, Passion, Death, and Resurrection of Our Lord Jesus Christ. § 2. Hope - Charity

q: What is hope?
a: Hope is that supernatural virtue by which we trust in God and expect from Him eternal life and the graces necessary to merit it here below by good works.

q: For what reason do we hope from God for eternal life and the graces necessary to merit it?
a: We hope from God for eternal life and the graces necessary to merit it because He, infinitely good and faithful, has promised them to us through the merits of Jesus Christ; therefore one who distrusts or despairs offends Him gravely.

q: What is charity?
a: Charity is that supernatural virtue by which we love God for Himself above all things, and our neighbor as ourselves for the love of God.

q: Why must we love God?
a: We must love God for Himself, as the supreme Good, the source of all our good; and therefore we must also love Him above all things "with all our heart, with all our soul, with all our mind, and with all our strength" (Mark XII. 30).

q: Why must we love our neighbor?
a: We must love our neighbor for the love of God, who commands it, and because every man is created in the image of God, as we are, and is our brother.

q: Are we bound to love even our enemies?
a: We are bound to love even our enemies, forgiving offenses, because they too are our neighbor, and because Jesus Christ has expressly commanded it.

q: When must we make acts of faith, hope, and charity?
a: We must make acts of faith, hope, and charity many times in life, and in particular when we have temptations to overcome or important Christian duties to fulfill, and in the dangers of death.

q: Is it good to make acts of faith, hope, and charity often?
a: It is good to make acts of faith, hope, and charity often, in order to preserve, increase, and strengthen virtues so necessary, which are like the vital parts of the "spiritual man."

q: How must we make acts of faith, hope, and charity?
a: We must make acts of faith, hope, and charity with the heart, with the mouth, and by works, giving proof of them in our conduct.

q: How does one give proof of faith?
a: One gives proof of faith by professing and defending it, when needed, without fear and without human respect, and by living according to its maxims: "faith without works is dead" (James II. 26).

q: How does one give proof of hope?
a: One gives proof of hope by not being troubled by the miseries and contrarieties of life, nor even by persecutions, but by living resigned, sure of the promises of God.

q: How does one give proof of charity?
a: One gives proof of charity by observing the commandments and exercising the works of mercy, and, if God calls, by following the evangelical counsels. 249 a. The seven corporal works of mercy: 1. To feed the hungry; 2. To give drink to the thirsty; 3. To clothe the naked; 4. To shelter the homeless; 5. To visit the sick; 6. To visit the imprisoned; 7. To bury the dead. 249 b. The seven spiritual works of mercy: 1. To counsel the doubtful; 2. To instruct the ignorant; 3. To admonish sinners; 4. To comfort the afflicted; 5. To forgive offences; 6. To bear wrongs patiently; 7. To pray for the living and the dead.

q: What are the evangelical counsels?
a: The evangelical counsels are exhortations that Jesus Christ made in the Gospel to a more perfect life, by the practice of virtues that are not commanded.

q: What are the principal evangelical counsels?
a: The principal evangelical counsels are: voluntary poverty, perpetual chastity, and perfect obedience. § 3. Moral Virtues and Vices — Evangelical Beatitudes

q: What is moral virtue?
a: Moral virtue is the habit of doing good, acquired by repeating good acts.

q: What are the principal moral virtues?
a: The principal moral virtues are: religion, which makes us render to God the worship due to Him, and the four cardinal virtues — prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance — which make us upright in our living.

q: Why are the cardinal virtues so called?
a: The cardinal virtues are so called because they are the hinge — that is, the support — of the other moral virtues.

q: What is prudence?
a: Prudence is the virtue that directs acts to their due end, and makes us discern and use good means.

q: What is justice?
a: Justice is the virtue that makes us give to each one what is due to him.

q: What is fortitude?
a: Fortitude is the virtue that makes us face, without rashness and without timidity, any difficulty or danger, and even death, for the service of God and for the good of our neighbor.

q: What is temperance?
a: Temperance is the virtue that bridles the passions and the desires, especially the sensual ones, and moderates the use of the goods perceived by the senses.

q: What are the passions?
a: The passions are emotions or violent movements of the soul which, if not moderated by reason, drag us toward vice and often even toward crime.

q: What is vice?
a: Vice is the habit of doing evil, acquired by repeating evil acts.

q: What are the principal vices?
a: The principal vices are the seven capital vices, so called because they are the head and the origin of the other vices and sins. 261 a. The seven capital sins: 1. Pride; 2. Covetousness; 3. Lust; 4. Anger; 5. Gluttony; 6. Envy; 7. Sloth.

q: What are the virtues opposed to the capital vices?
a: The virtues opposed to the capital vices are: humility, liberality, chastity, patience, sobriety, fraternity, and diligence in the service of God.

q: Did Jesus Christ recommend any moral virtue in particular?
a: Jesus Christ recommended in particular some moral virtues, calling blessed, in the eight Evangelical Beatitudes, those who would practice them.

q: Recite the Evangelical Beatitudes.
a: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are they who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure of heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God. Blessed are they who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V. 3-10).

q: Why did Jesus Christ, in the Evangelical Beatitudes, call blessed — contrary to the opinion of the world — the humble and the afflicted?
a: Jesus Christ, in the Evangelical Beatitudes, called blessed — contrary to the opinion of the world — the humble and the afflicted, because they will have a special reward from God; and He taught us also to imitate them, without heeding the deceitful maxims of the world.

q: Can those who follow the maxims of the world be truly happy?
a: Those who follow the maxims of the world cannot be truly happy, because they do not seek God, their Lord and their true happiness; and so they have no peace of conscience, and walk toward perdition.

q: What are the sacraments?
a: The sacraments are efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Jesus Christ to sanctify us.

q: Why are the sacraments efficacious signs of grace?
a: The sacraments are signs of grace because, by the perceptible part they have, they signify or indicate the invisible grace they confer; and they are efficacious signs of grace because, signifying grace, they really confer it.

q: What grace do the sacraments confer?
a: The sacraments confer sanctifying grace and sacramental grace.

q: What is sanctifying grace?
a: Sanctifying grace is that supernatural gift, inherent in our soul and therefore habitual, which makes us holy — that is, just, friends and adopted children of God, brothers of Jesus Christ, and heirs of heaven.

q: What is sacramental grace?
a: Sacramental grace is the right to the special graces necessary to attain the proper end of each sacrament.

q: Who gave to the sacraments the power to confer grace?
a: Jesus Christ, the Man-God, gave to the sacraments the power to confer grace, which He Himself merited for us by His Passion and Death.

q: How do the sacraments sanctify us?
a: The sacraments sanctify us either by giving us the first sanctifying grace, which blots out sin, or by increasing in us the grace we already possess.

q: Which sacraments give us the first grace?
a: The sacraments that give us the first grace are Baptism and Penance, which are called sacraments of the dead, because they give the life of grace to souls dead through sin.

q: Which sacraments increase grace in us?
a: The sacraments that increase grace in us are Confirmation, the Eucharist, Extreme Unction, Holy Orders, and Matrimony, which are called sacraments of the living, because whoever receives them must already live spiritually by the grace of God.

q: Does one who receives a sacrament of the living, knowing he is not in the grace of God, commit a sin?
a: One who receives a sacrament of the living, knowing he is not in the grace of God, commits a most grave sin of sacrilege, because he receives a sacred thing unworthily.

q: What must we do to preserve the grace of the sacraments?
a: To preserve the grace of the sacraments we must correspond by our own action, doing good and avoiding evil.

q: Which are the sacraments most necessary for salvation?
a: The sacraments most necessary for salvation are the sacraments of the dead, that is, Baptism and Penance, because they give the first grace, or the spiritual life.

q: Are Baptism and Penance equally necessary?
a: Baptism and Penance are not equally necessary, because Baptism is necessary for all, since all are born with original sin; Penance, on the other hand, is necessary for those who, after Baptism, have lost grace by sinning mortally.

q: If Baptism is necessary for all, can no one be saved without Baptism?
a: Without Baptism no one can be saved; however, when Baptism of water cannot be received, Baptism of blood — that is, martyrdom suffered for Jesus Christ — suffices, or Baptism of desire, which is the love of charity, desirous of the means of salvation instituted by God.

q: How many times can the sacraments be received?
a: Some sacraments can be received many times; others only once.

q: Which sacraments are received only once?
a: Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders are received only once.

q: Why are Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders received only once?
a: Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders are received only once because they imprint on the soul a permanent character, working a perpetual consecration of the man to Jesus Christ, which distinguishes him from one who has not received them.

q: What is the character?
a: The character is a spiritual distinguishing sign that is never effaced.

q: What character do Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders imprint on the soul?
a: Baptism imprints on the soul the character of a Christian; Confirmation, that of a soldier of Jesus Christ; Holy Orders, that of His minister.

q: How many things are required to make a sacrament?
a: Three things are required to make a sacrament: the matter, the form, and the minister, who must have the intention of doing what the Church does.

q: What is the matter of the sacrament?
a: The matter of the sacrament is the perceptible element required in order to make it, such as water in Baptism.

q: What is the form of the sacrament?
a: The form of the sacrament is the words that the minister must pronounce at the very moment of applying the matter.

q: Who is the minister of the sacrament?
a: The minister of the sacrament is the qualified person who makes or confers it, in the name and by the authority of Jesus Christ.

q: What is Baptism?
a: Baptism is the sacrament that makes us Christians, that is, followers of Jesus Christ, children of God, and members of the Church.

q: What is the matter of Baptism?
a: The matter of Baptism is natural water.

q: What is the form of Baptism?
a: The form of Baptism is the words: "I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit."

q: Who is the minister of Baptism?
a: The minister of Baptism is ordinarily the priest; but in case of necessity it can be anyone, even a heretic or an unbeliever, provided he has the intention of doing what the Church does.

q: How is Baptism given?
a: Baptism is given by pouring water on the head of the one being baptized while pronouncing at the same time the words of the form.

q: What effects does Baptism produce?
a: Baptism confers the first sanctifying grace and the supernatural virtues, taking away original sin and any actual sins, with every debt of punishment due for them; it imprints the character of a Christian and makes one capable of receiving the other sacraments.

q: Does Baptism transform man?
a: Baptism transforms man in the spirit and causes him, as it were, to be reborn, making him a new man; for this reason a fitting name is then given to him, that of a Saint who is to be his example and protector in his life as a Christian.

q: To what does one who receives Baptism bind himself?
a: One who receives Baptism, becoming a Christian, binds himself to profess the Faith and to observe the Law of Jesus Christ; and therefore he renounces whatever is opposed to them.

q: What does one renounce in receiving Baptism?
a: In receiving Baptism, one renounces the devil, his works, and his pomps.

q: What is meant by the works and pomps of the devil?
a: By the works and pomps of the devil are meant sins, the vanities of the world, and its perverse maxims, contrary to the Gospel.

q: How do children renounce the devil at Baptism?
a: Children at Baptism renounce the devil through their godparents.

q: Who are the godparents at Baptism?
a: The godparents at Baptism are those who present the one to be baptized to the Church, answer in his name if he is a child, and undertake, as spiritual parents, the care of his Christian upbringing should the parents fail in it; and for this reason they must be good Christians.

q: Are we bound to keep the promises and renunciations made by our godparents in our name at Baptism?
a: We are bound to keep the promises and renunciations made by our godparents in our name at Baptism, because they impose on us only what God imposes on all, and what we ourselves would have to promise in order to be saved.

q: When must parents, or those who take their place, send the child to be baptized?
a: Parents, or those who take their place, must send the child to be baptized no later than eight or ten days; indeed, it is fitting to secure for him grace and eternal happiness at once, since he might very easily die.

q: What is Confirmation?
a: Confirmation is the sacrament that makes us perfect Christians and soldiers of Jesus Christ, and imprints in us its character.

q: What is the matter of Confirmation?
a: The matter of Confirmation is the holy chrism, that is, oil mixed with balsam, consecrated by the Bishop on Holy Thursday.

q: What is the form of Confirmation?
a: The form of Confirmation is the words: "I sign you with the sign of the Cross, and confirm you with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit."

q: Who is the minister of Confirmation?
a: The minister of Confirmation is the Bishop, and, extraordinarily, the priest who has the faculty for it from the Pope.

q: How does the Bishop administer Confirmation?
a: The Bishop, having extended his hands over those to be confirmed, invokes the Holy Spirit; then with the holy chrism he anoints in the form of a cross the forehead of each one, pronouncing the words of the form; he then gives each a slight tap on the cheek, saying: "Peace be with you"; and at the end he solemnly blesses all those who have been confirmed.

q: In what way does Confirmation make us perfect Christians and soldiers of Jesus Christ?
a: Confirmation makes us perfect Christians and soldiers of Jesus Christ by giving us the abundance of the Holy Spirit, that is, of His grace and of His gifts, which confirm or strengthen us in faith and in the other virtues against our spiritual enemies.

q: At what age is it good to receive Confirmation?
a: It is good to receive Confirmation at about seven years of age, because then temptations usually begin, and one can sufficiently know the holiness and the grace of this sacrament.

q: What dispositions must one who receives Confirmation have?
a: One who receives Confirmation must be in the grace of God; and, if he has the use of reason, he must know the principal mysteries of the Faith, and approach the sacrament with devotion, deeply imbued with what the rite signifies.

q: What does the holy chrism signify?
a: The holy chrism, with the oil that spreads and gives strength, signifies the abundant grace of Confirmation; and with the balsam, which is fragrant and preserves from corruption, signifies the good odor of the virtues that the confirmed person must possess, fleeing from the corruption of the vices.

q: What does the anointing made on the forehead in the form of a cross signify?
a: The anointing made on the forehead in the form of a cross signifies that the confirmed person, as a strong soldier of Jesus Christ, must hold his forehead high, without blushing for the Cross and without fear of the enemies of the Faith.

q: What does the slight tap that the Bishop gives the confirmed person signify?
a: The slight tap that the Bishop gives the confirmed person signifies that he must be ready to suffer every affront and every pain for the Faith.

q: Are there godparents at Confirmation?
a: At Confirmation there are godfathers for men and godmothers for women, who must be good Christians, in order to edify and spiritually assist the newly confirmed.

q: What is the Eucharist?
a: The Eucharist is the sacrament that, under the appearances of bread and wine, really contains the Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ for the nourishment of souls.

q: What is the matter of the Eucharist?
a: The matter of the Eucharist is wheat bread and wine of the grape.

q: What is the form of the Eucharist?
a: The form of the Eucharist is the words of Jesus Christ: "This is my Body; this is the chalice of my Blood ... shed for you and for many unto the remission of sins."

q: Who is the minister of the Eucharist?
a: The minister of the Eucharist is the priest, who, by pronouncing in the Mass the words of Jesus Christ, changes the bread into His Body and the wine into His Blood.

q: When did Jesus Christ institute the Eucharist?
a: Jesus Christ instituted the Eucharist at the Last Supper, before His Passion, when He consecrated bread and wine and distributed them to the Apostles as His Body and Blood, commanding that they should afterward do the same in His memory.

q: Why did Jesus Christ institute the Eucharist?
a: Jesus Christ instituted the Eucharist so that it might be in the Mass the permanent sacrifice of the New Testament, and in Communion the food of souls, in perpetual remembrance of His love and of His Passion and Death.

q: Is the same Jesus Christ in the Eucharist who is in heaven and who was born on earth of the Virgin Mary?
a: In the Eucharist is the same Jesus Christ who is in heaven and who was born on earth of the Virgin Mary.

q: Why do you believe that Jesus Christ is truly in the Eucharist?
a: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly in the Eucharist because He Himself called the consecrated bread and wine His Body and Blood, and because the Church teaches us so; but it is a mystery, and a great mystery.

q: What is the host before the consecration?
a: The host before the consecration is bread.

q: After the consecration, what is the host?
a: After the consecration, the host is the true Body of Our Lord Jesus Christ under the appearances of bread.

q: What is contained in the chalice before the consecration?
a: Before the consecration, the chalice contains wine with a few drops of water.

q: What is in the chalice after the consecration?
a: In the chalice after the consecration is the true Blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ under the appearances of wine.

q: When do the bread and the wine become the Body and Blood of Jesus?
a: The bread and the wine become the Body and Blood of Jesus at the moment of the consecration.

q: After the consecration, is there nothing left of the bread and wine?
a: After the consecration, there is no longer either bread or wine, but only the species or appearances remain, without the substance.

q: What are the species or appearances?
a: The species or appearances are all that falls under the senses, such as the figure, the color, the odor, and the taste of bread and wine.

q: Under the appearances of bread is there only the Body of Jesus Christ, or under those of wine only His Blood?
a: No: under the appearances of bread is the whole Jesus Christ, in Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity; and so also under those of wine.

q: When the host is broken into many parts, is the Body of Jesus Christ broken?
a: When the host is broken into many parts, the Body of Jesus Christ is not broken, but only the species of bread; and the Body of the Lord remains whole in each part.

q: Is Jesus Christ found in all the consecrated hosts of the world?
a: Yes, Jesus Christ is found in all the consecrated hosts of the world.

q: Why is the Most Holy Eucharist preserved in churches?
a: The Most Holy Eucharist is preserved in churches so that the faithful may adore it, may receive it in Communion, and may sense in it the perpetual assistance and presence of Jesus Christ in the Church. § 3. Holy Communion: Dispositions, Obligation, Effects

q: How many things are necessary to make a good Communion?
a: To make a good Communion three things are necessary: 1. to be in the grace of God; 2. to know and to think about whom one is going to receive; 3. to be fasting from midnight.

q: What does "to be in the grace of God" mean?
a: To be in the grace of God means to have one's conscience clean of every mortal sin.

q: Does one who receives Communion knowing that he is in mortal sin receive Jesus Christ?
a: One who receives Communion knowing that he is in mortal sin does receive Jesus Christ, but not His grace; rather, by committing a horrible sacrilege, he renders himself deserving of damnation.

q: What does "to know and to think about whom one is going to receive" mean?
a: To know and to think about whom one is going to receive means to approach Our Lord Jesus Christ in the Eucharist with living faith, with ardent desire, and with deep humility and modesty.

q: What fast is required before Communion?
a: Before Communion the natural — that is, total — fast is required, which is broken by anything taken in the manner of food or drink.

q: Is Communion ever permitted to one who is not fasting?
a: Communion is permitted to one who is not fasting in danger of death, and during long illnesses, under the conditions determined by the Church.

q: Is there an obligation to receive Communion?
a: There is an obligation to receive Communion every year at Easter, and in danger of death, as Viaticum, to sustain the soul on its journey to eternity.

q: At what age does the obligation of the Easter Communion begin?
a: The obligation of the Easter Communion begins at the age at which one is capable of making it with sufficient dispositions, that is, ordinarily about the seventh year.

q: Is it good and useful to receive Communion often?
a: It is most good and most useful to receive Communion often, even every day, provided one always does so with the proper dispositions.

q: After Communion, how long does Jesus Christ remain in us?
a: After Communion, Jesus Christ remains in us as long as the eucharistic species last.

q: What effects does the Eucharist produce in one who receives it worthily?
a: The Eucharist, in one who receives it worthily, preserves and increases the grace that is the life of the soul, as food does for the life of the body; remits venial sins and preserves from mortal ones; gives spiritual consolation and comfort, increasing charity and the hope of eternal life, of which it is the pledge.

q: Is the Eucharist only a sacrament?
a: The Eucharist is not only a sacrament, but is also the permanent sacrifice of the New Testament, and as such is called the Holy Mass.

q: What is sacrifice?
a: Sacrifice is the public offering to God of a thing that is destroyed in order to profess that He is the Creator and supreme Master, to whom everything entirely is due.

q: What is the Holy Mass?
a: The Holy Mass is the sacrifice of the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ which, under the species of bread and wine, is offered by the priest to God upon the altar, in memory and renewal of the sacrifice of the Cross.

q: Is the sacrifice of the Mass the same sacrifice as that of the Cross?
a: The sacrifice of the Mass is the same sacrifice as that of the Cross; there is only a difference in the manner of accomplishing it.

q: What difference is there between the sacrifice of the Cross and that of the Mass?
a: Between the sacrifice of the Cross and that of the Mass there is this difference: that Jesus Christ on the Cross sacrificed Himself by voluntarily giving His own Blood, and merited every grace for us; whereas on the altar He, without shedding blood, sacrifices and annihilates Himself mystically through the ministry of the priest, and applies to us the merits of the sacrifice of the Cross.

q: For what ends is the Mass offered to God?
a: The Mass is offered to God in order to render Him supreme worship of latria or adoration, to thank Him for His benefits, to appease Him and to give Him satisfaction for our sins, and to obtain graces for the benefit of the faithful living and departed.

q: Is the Mass not also offered to the Saints?
a: The Mass is not offered to the Saints, but to God alone, even when it is celebrated in honor of the Saints: sacrifice belongs only to the Creator and supreme Master.

q: Are we bound to hear Mass?
a: We are bound to hear Mass on Sundays and on the other commanded feast days; but it is profitable to assist at it often, in order to share in the greatest act of religion, supremely pleasing to God and meritorious.

q: What is the most fitting way to assist at Mass?
a: The most fitting way to assist at Mass is to offer it to God in union with the priest, recalling the sacrifice of the Cross — that is, the Passion and Death of the Lord — and receiving Communion: Communion is real union with the immolated Victim, and is therefore the greatest sharing in the Holy Sacrifice.

q: What is Penance?
a: Penance, or Confession, is the sacrament instituted by Jesus Christ to forgive the sins committed after Baptism.

q: When was the sacrament of Penance instituted by Jesus Christ?
a: The sacrament of Penance was instituted by Jesus Christ when He said to the Apostles, and in them to their successors: "Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained" (John XX. 22-23).

q: Who is the minister of Penance?
a: The minister of Penance is the priest approved by the Bishop.

q: How many and what things are required to make a good confession?
a: To make a good confession five things are required: 1. the examination of conscience; 2. sorrow for sins; 3. the resolution to commit them no more; 4. the confession; 5. satisfaction or penance.

q: How is the examination of conscience made?
a: The examination of conscience is made by recalling to mind the sins committed in thoughts, words, deeds, and omissions, against the commandments of God, the precepts of the Church, and the obligations of one's state in life, beginning from the last well-made confession.

q: In the examination must we seek out the number of our sins?
a: In the examination we must diligently seek out also the number of our mortal sins.

q: What is sorrow?
a: Sorrow, or repentance, is that displeasure with and hatred of the sins committed which makes us resolve not to sin again.

q: How many kinds of sorrow are there?
a: Sorrow is of two kinds: perfect, or contrition; and imperfect, or attrition.

q: What is perfect sorrow, or contrition?
a: Perfect sorrow, or contrition, is the displeasure for the sins committed because they are an offense against God our Father, infinitely good and lovable, and the cause of the Passion and Death of Our Redeemer Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

q: Why is contrition perfect sorrow?
a: Contrition is perfect sorrow because it springs from a perfect motive — the filial love of God, or charity — and because it obtains for us at once the forgiveness of sins, although the obligation of confessing them remains.

q: What is imperfect sorrow, or attrition?
a: Imperfect sorrow, or attrition, is the displeasure for the sins committed, out of fear of eternal and temporal punishments, or also because of the ugliness of sin.

q: Why is attrition imperfect sorrow?
a: Attrition is imperfect sorrow because it springs from less perfect motives — those proper to servants rather than to children — and because it does not obtain for us the forgiveness of sins except through the sacrament.

q: Is it necessary to have sorrow for all the sins committed?
a: It is necessary to have sorrow for all the mortal sins committed, without exception; and it is fitting to have sorrow also for the venial ones.

q: Why is it necessary to have sorrow for all mortal sins?
a: It is necessary to have sorrow for all mortal sins because by any one of them we have gravely offended God, lost His grace, and merited to remain separated from Him forever.

q: What is the resolution?
a: The resolution is the firm will never again to commit sins and to flee their occasions.

q: What is the occasion of sin?
a: The occasion of sin is whatever puts us in danger of sinning, whether a person or a thing.

q: Are we bound to flee the occasions of sins?
a: We are bound to flee the occasions of sins, because we are bound to flee sin: whoever does not flee them ends by falling, since "he who loves danger will perish in it" (Ecclus. III. 27).

q: What is confession?
a: Confession is the accusation of one's sins made to the priest confessor, in order to receive absolution.

q: Of what sins are we bound to confess?
a: We are bound to confess all mortal sins not yet confessed, or confessed badly; but it is profitable to confess venial sins also.

q: How must we accuse our mortal sins?
a: We must accuse our mortal sins fully, without letting ourselves be overcome by a false shame to keep any silent, declaring their kind, their number, and also the circumstances that would add a new grave malice.

q: What must one do who does not remember the precise number of his mortal sins?
a: One who does not remember the precise number of his mortal sins must indicate the number that seems to him closest to the truth.

q: Why must we not let ourselves be overcome by shame to keep silent some mortal sin?
a: We must not let ourselves be overcome by shame to keep silent some mortal sin, because we confess to Jesus Christ in the person of the confessor, and the confessor cannot reveal any sin, even at the cost of his life; and because, otherwise, not obtaining forgiveness, we shall be put to shame before all at the universal judgment.

q: Would one who through shame or some other motive kept silent a mortal sin make a good confession?
a: One who through shame or any other unjust motive kept silent a mortal sin would not make a good confession, but would commit a sacrilege.

q: What must one do who knows he has not confessed well?
a: One who knows he has not confessed well must repeat the badly made confessions and accuse himself of the sacrileges committed.

q: Has one made a good confession who without fault left out or forgot a mortal sin?
a: One who without fault left out or forgot a mortal sin has made a good confession; but the obligation remains for him to accuse himself of it afterward. § 4. Absolution — Satisfaction — Indulgences

q: What is absolution?
a: Absolution is the sentence by which the priest, in the name of Jesus Christ, forgives the penitent's sins, saying: "I absolve you from your sins, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen."

q: When sins are forgiven by absolution, is also every punishment merited forgiven?
a: When sins are forgiven by absolution, the eternal punishment merited by mortal sin is forgiven; but unless one has the most perfect contrition, there ordinarily remains, to be paid in this life or in the next, a temporal punishment.

q: What is satisfaction, or sacramental penance?
a: Satisfaction, or sacramental penance, is the good work imposed by the confessor as a chastisement and correction of the sinner, and to pay off the temporal punishment merited by sinning.

q: When is it fitting to perform sacramental penance?
a: It is fitting to perform sacramental penance as soon as possible, if the confessor has not assigned a specific time for it.

q: Does sacramental penance suffice to free us from all the temporal punishment merited by sin?
a: Sacramental penance does not, ordinarily, suffice to free us from all the temporal punishment merited by sin; and therefore it is fitting to make up for it by other works of penance and piety, and by indulgences.

q: What are the works of penance and of piety?
a: The works of penance and of piety are: fasting, mortifications, the acts of spiritual and corporal mercy, prayers, and the devout use of those blessed things and those sacred ceremonies which are called sacramentals, such as holy water and the various blessings. 385 a. The seven corporal works of mercy: 1. To feed the hungry; 2. To give drink to the thirsty; 3. To clothe the naked; 4. To shelter the homeless; 5. To visit the sick; 6. To visit the imprisoned; 7. To bury the dead. 385 b. The seven spiritual works of mercy: 1. To counsel the doubtful; 2. To instruct the ignorant; 3. To admonish sinners; 4. To comfort the afflicted; 5. To forgive offences; 6. To bear wrongs patiently; 7. To pray for the living and the dead.

q: What is an indulgence?
a: An indulgence is a remission of the temporal punishment due for sins, which the Church grants under certain conditions to one who is in grace, by applying to him the superabundant merits and satisfactions of Jesus Christ, of Our Lady, and of the Saints, which constitute the treasury of the Church.

q: How many kinds of indulgence are there?
a: Indulgence is of two kinds: plenary and partial.

q: What is the plenary indulgence?
a: The plenary indulgence is the one that remits all the temporal punishment due for sins.

q: What is the partial indulgence?
a: The partial indulgence is the one that remits only a part of the temporal punishment due for sins.

q: What is meant by an indulgence of "forty" or "a hundred days," of "seven years," and the like?
a: By an indulgence of forty or a hundred days, of seven years, and the like, is meant the remission of as much temporal punishment as would have been paid off by forty days, a hundred days, or seven years of the penance anciently established by the Church.

q: What is required to gain indulgences?
a: To gain indulgences it is required to be in the state of grace and to perform well the prescribed works.

q: What is Extreme Unction?
a: Extreme Unction, also called Holy Oil, is the sacrament instituted for the spiritual — and also bodily — relief of Christians who are gravely ill.

q: Who is the minister of Extreme Unction?
a: The minister of Extreme Unction is the parish priest, or another priest who has permission for it.

q: How does the priest administer Extreme Unction?
a: The priest administers Extreme Unction by anointing in the form of a cross, with oil blessed by the Bishop, the organs of the senses of the sick person, saying: "By this holy anointing and by His most loving mercy, may the Lord forgive you every fault committed by sight, by hearing, etc. Amen."

q: What effects does Extreme Unction produce?
a: Extreme Unction increases sanctifying grace; it blots out venial sins, and even mortal sins that the sick person, being only attrite, cannot confess; it gives strength to bear illness patiently, to resist temptations, and to die a holy death; and it also helps to restore health, if it is good for the soul.

q: When can Holy Oil be given?
a: Holy Oil can be given when the illness is dangerous; and it is good to give it immediately after confession and Viaticum, while the sick person retains his awareness.

q: What is "Holy Orders"?
a: Holy Orders is the sacrament that gives the power to perform the sacred actions concerning the Eucharist and the salvation of souls, and imprints the character of ministers of God.

q: Who is the minister of Holy Orders?
a: The minister of Holy Orders is the Bishop, who gives the Holy Spirit and the sacred power by imposing his hands and handing over the sacred objects proper to the Order, while pronouncing the words of the prescribed form.

q: Why is the sacrament that makes the ministers of God called Order?
a: The sacrament that makes the ministers of God is called Order because it includes various grades of ministers, one subordinate to another, from which results the sacred Hierarchy.

q: What are the grades of the sacred Hierarchy?
a: The grades of the sacred Hierarchy are: the minor Orders, the Subdiaconate, and the Diaconate, which are preparatory; the Presbyterate or Priesthood, which gives the power to consecrate the Eucharist and to forgive sins; and the Episcopate, the fullness of the Priesthood, which gives the power to confer Orders and to teach and govern the faithful.

q: Is the dignity of the Priesthood great?
a: The dignity of the Priesthood is most great, because of its power over the real Body of Jesus Christ, which it makes present in the Eucharist, and over His mystical body, the Church, which it governs, with the sublime mission of leading men to holiness and to the blessed life.

q: What end must one who enters Holy Orders have?
a: One who enters Holy Orders must have for his end solely the glory of God and the salvation of souls.

q: Can anyone enter Holy Orders of his own choice?
a: No one can enter Holy Orders of his own choice, but must be called by God through his own Bishop; that is, he must have the vocation, with the virtues and the aptitudes for the sacred ministry that the vocation requires.

q: Would one who entered the Priesthood without a vocation do wrong?
a: One who entered the Priesthood without a vocation would do very wrong, because he could only with difficulty observe its most exalted duties, with evident danger of public scandal and of eternal perdition.

q: What duties have the faithful toward those called to Holy Orders?
a: The faithful have the duty of leaving to their children and dependents full freedom to follow their vocation; also of asking God for good pastors and ministers, and of fasting for this end on the four Ember Days; finally, of venerating the ordained as persons consecrated to God.

q: What is Matrimony?
a: Matrimony is the sacrament that unites man and woman indissolubly, as Jesus Christ and the Church His spouse are united, and gives them the grace to live together in holiness and to raise their children in a Christian way.

q: Who is the minister of Matrimony?
a: The ministers of Matrimony are the spouses who contract it.

q: How is Matrimony contracted?
a: Matrimony is contracted by expressing the mutual consent before the parish priest, or a priest delegated by him, and at least two witnesses.

q: Does Matrimony celebrated in this form also obtain civil effects in Italy?
a: Matrimony celebrated in this form also obtains civil effects in Italy, because the Italian State recognizes such effects in the Sacrament of Matrimony.

q: How does Matrimony so celebrated obtain civil effects in Italy?
a: Matrimony so celebrated obtains civil effects in Italy through its regular transcription in the registers of the civil state, made at the request of the parish priest.

q: Can Catholic spouses also perform a civil marriage?
a: Catholic spouses cannot perform a civil marriage either before or after the religious Matrimony; should they dare to do so even with the intention of celebrating the religious Matrimony afterward, they are considered by the Church to be public sinners.

q: Must the spouses be in the grace of God when contracting Matrimony?
a: The spouses must be in the grace of God when contracting Matrimony; otherwise they commit a sacrilege.

q: What duties have the spouses?
a: The spouses have the duty to live together in holiness, to help one another with constant affection in their spiritual and temporal needs, and to raise their children well, caring for their soul no less than for their body, and forming them above all in religion and in virtue by word and by example.

q: What is prayer?
a: Prayer is a pious raising of the soul to God in order to know Him well, to adore Him, to thank Him, and to ask Him for what we need.

q: How many kinds of prayer are there?
a: There are two kinds of prayer: mental and vocal.

q: What is mental prayer?
a: Mental prayer is that which is made with the mind and the heart alone: such are the meditation of the Christian truths, and contemplation.

q: What is vocal prayer?
a: Vocal prayer, more commonly called simply "prayer," is that which is made with words accompanied by the mind and the heart.

q: How must we pray?
a: We must pray reflecting that we are in the presence of the infinite majesty of God, and that we are in need of His mercy; and therefore we must be humble, attentive, and devout.

q: Is it necessary to pray?
a: It is necessary to pray, and to pray often, because God commands it; and ordinarily it is only when one prays that He grants spiritual and temporal graces.

q: Why does God grant the graces we ask of Him?
a: God grants the graces we ask of Him because He, who is most faithful, has promised to hear us if we pray with confidence and perseverance in the name of Jesus Christ.

q: Why must we pray to God in the name of Jesus Christ?
a: We must pray to God in the name of Jesus Christ, because only through Him, His Son and the one Mediator between God and men, do our prayers and good works have value; for this reason the Church is accustomed to end her prayers with these or equivalent words: "through your Son Jesus Christ, Our Lord."

q: Why are we not always heard in our prayers?
a: We are not always heard in our prayers either because we pray badly, or because we ask for things not useful to our true good, that is, to our spiritual good.

q: What things must we ask of God?
a: We must ask of God His glory, and for ourselves eternal life and even temporal graces, as Jesus Christ has taught us in the Our Father.

q: What is the Our Father?
a: The Our Father is the prayer taught and recommended by Jesus Christ; it is therefore called the Lord's Prayer, and it is the most excellent of all prayers.

q: Why is the Our Father the most excellent prayer?
a: The Our Father is the most excellent prayer because it came forth from the mind and Heart of Jesus, and contains in seven brief petitions all that we must ask of God as His children and as brothers among ourselves.

q: What must we ask as good children of God?
a: As good children of God we must ask that throughout the world His name be known and honored, that His kingdom — the Church — be spread, and that His most holy will be fulfilled by all: this is what is asked in the first three petitions of the Our Father.

q: As brothers among ourselves, what must we ask?
a: As brothers among ourselves we must ask for bodily and spiritual nourishment, the forgiveness of sins, the defense from temptations, and the deliverance from evil: this is what is asked, for ourselves and for all human beings, in the last four petitions of the Our Father.

q: Why does Jesus Christ have us call upon God as "Our Father"?
a: Jesus Christ has us call upon God as "Our Father" to remind us that God is truly the Father of all, especially of us Christians who, in Baptism, were adopted by Him as His children; and to inspire in us a great love and confidence toward Him.

q: If God hears one who prays well, why do we also call upon Our Lady, the Angels, and the Saints?
a: We also call upon Our Lady, the Angels, and the Saints because, being dear to the Lord and merciful toward us, they may help us in our petitions by their powerful intercession.

q: Why are the Angels, the Saints, and Our Lady powerful intercessors before God?
a: The Angels and the Saints are powerful intercessors before God because they are His faithful servants, indeed His chosen friends; Our Lady is most powerful because she is the Mother of God and full of grace, and for this reason we call upon her so often, all the more since she was left to us as our Mother by Jesus Christ.

q: With what prayer especially do we call upon Our Lady?
a: We call upon Our Lady especially with the Hail Mary, or Angelic Salutation, so called because it begins with the greeting that the Archangel Gabriel made to her when announcing that she was chosen to be the Mother of God.

q: What do we ask of Our Lady in the Hail Mary?
a: In the Hail Mary we ask Our Lady for her motherly intercession for us in life and in death.

q: Does the invocation of Our Lady and of the Saints not perhaps show distrust in Jesus Christ, the one Mediator, as if His merits were not enough to obtain graces for us?
a: The invocation of Our Lady and of the Saints shows no distrust in Jesus Christ, the one Mediator; on the contrary, it shows a greater faith in His merits, so great and so efficacious that through them, and only through them, Our Lady and the Saints have from God grace, merits, and the power of intercession.
